[1.] He calls her <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> not mother, not out of any disrespect to her, but because mother would have been a cutting word to her that was already wounded to the heart with grief; like Isaac saying to Abraham, <hi type="italic">My father.</hi> He speaks as one that was <hi type="italic">now no more in this world,</hi> but was already dead to those in it that were dearest to him. His speaking in this seemingly slight manner to his mother, as he had done formerly, was designed to obviate and give a check to the undue honours which he foresaw would be given to her in the Romish church, as if she were a joint purchaser with him in the honours of the Redeemer. [2.] He directs her to look upon John as her son: "Behold him as thy son, who stands there by thee, and be as a mother to him." See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> An instance of divine goodness, to be observed for our encouragement. Sometimes, when God removes one comfort from us, he raises up another for us, perhaps where we looked not for it. We read of children which the church shall have after she has lost the other, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa. xlix. 21</reference>. Let none therefore reckon all gone with one cistern dried up, for from the same fountain another may be filled. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> An instance of filial duty, to be observed for our imitation. Christ has here taught children to provide, to the utmost of their power, for the comfort of their aged parents. When David was in distress, he took care of his parents, and found out a shelter for them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3">1 Sam. xxii. 3</reference>); so the Son of David here. Children at their death, according to their ability, should provide for their parents, if they survive them, and need their kindness. <div eID="gen28603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28604" type="x-p"/> (2.) The confidence he reposed in the beloved disciple. It is to him he says, <hi type="italic">Behold thy mother,</hi> that is, I recommend her to thy care, be thou as a son to her to guide her (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.18">Isa. li. 18</reference>); and <hi type="italic">forsake her not when she is old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.22">Prov. xxiii. 22</reference>. Now, [1.] This was an honour put upon John, and a testimony both to his prudence and to his fidelity. If he who knows all things had not known that John loved him, he would not have made him his mother's guardian. It is a great honour to be employed for Christ, and to be entrusted with any of his interest in the world. But, [2.] It would be a care and some charge to John; but he cheerfully accepted it, <hi type="italic">and took her to his own home,</hi> not objecting the trouble nor expense, nor his obligations to his own family, nor the ill-will he might contract by it. Note, Those that truly love Christ, and are beloved of him, will be glad of an opportunity to do any service to him or his. <hi type="italic">Nicephoras's Eccl. Hist. lib. 2 cap. 3,</hi> saith that the virgin Mary lived with John at Jerusalem eleven years, and then died. Others, that she lived to remove with him to Ephesus. <div eID="gen28604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28605" type="x-p"/> IV. The fulfilling of the scripture, in the giving of him vinegar to drink, <reference osisRef="John.19.28-John.19.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28606" type="x-p"/> 1. How much respect Christ showed to the scripture (<reference osisRef="John.19.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Knowing that all things</hi> hitherto <hi type="italic">were accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled,</hi> which spoke of his drinking in his sufferings, <hi type="italic">he saith, I thirst,</hi> that is, he called for drink. <div eID="gen28606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28607" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was not at all strange that he was thirsty; we find him <hi type="italic">thirsty</hi> in a journey (<reference osisRef="John.4.6-John.4.7">ch. iv. 6, 7</reference>), and now thirsty when he was just at his journey's end. Well might he thirst after all the toil and hurry which he had undergone, and being now in the agonies of death, ready to expire purely by the loss of blood and extremity of pain. The torments of hell are represented by a violent thirst in the complaint of the rich man that begged for a <hi type="italic">drop of water to cool his tongue.</hi> To that everlasting thirst we had been condemned, had not Christ suffered for us. <div eID="gen28607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28608" type="x-p"/> (2.) But the reason of his complaining of it is somewhat surprising; it is the only word he spoke that looked like complaint of his outward sufferings. When they scourged him, and crowned him with thorns, he did not cry, O my head! or, My back! But now he cried, <hi type="italic">I thirst.</hi> For, [1.] He would thus express <hi type="italic">the travail of his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. He thirsted after the glorifying of God, and the accomplishment of the work of our redemption, and the happy issue of his undertaking. [2.] He would thus take care to see the scripture fulfilled. Hitherto, all had been accomplished, and he knew it, for this was the thing he had carefully observed all along; and now he called to mind one thing more, which this was the proper season for the performance of. By this it appears that he was the Messiah, in that not only the scripture was punctually fulfilled in him, but it was strictly eyed by him. By this it appears <hi type="italic">that God was with him of a truth</hi>—that in all he did he went exactly according to the word of God, taking care <hi type="italic">not to destroy, but to fulfil, the law and the prophets.</hi> Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The scripture had foretold his thirst, and therefore he himself related it, because it could not otherwise be known, saying, <hi type="italic">I thirst;</hi> it was foretold that his tongue should cleave to his jaws, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Ps. xxii. 15</reference>. Samson, an eminent type of Christ, when he was laying <hi type="italic">the Philistines heaps upon heaps,</hi> was himself <hi type="italic">sore athirst</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.15.18">Judg. xv. 18</reference>); so was Christ, when he was upon the cross, <hi type="italic">spoiling principalities and powers. Secondly,</hi> The scripture had foretold that in his thirst he should have vinegar given him to drink, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">Ps. lxix. 21</reference>. They had given him vinegar to drink before they crucified him (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.34">Matt. xxvii. 34</reference>), but the prophecy was not exactly fulfilled in that, because that was not in his thirst; therefore now he said, <hi type="italic">I thirst,</hi> and called for it again: then he would not drink, but now he received it Christ would rather court an affront than see any prophecy unfulfilled. This should satisfy us under all our trials, that the will of God is done, and the word of God accomplished. <div eID="gen28608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28609" type="x-p"/> 2. See how little respect his persecutors showed to him (<reference osisRef="John.19.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was set a vessel full of vinegar,</hi> probably according to the custom at all executions of this nature; or, as others think, it was now set designedly for an abuse to Christ, instead of the cup of wine which they used to give <hi type="italic">to those that were ready to perish;</hi> with this <hi type="italic">they filled a sponge,</hi> for they would not allow him a cup, <hi type="italic">and they put it upon hyssop,</hi> a hyssop-stalk, and with this heaved it to his mouth; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyssopo perithentes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they stuck it round with hyssop;</hi> so it may be taken; or, as others, they mingled it with hyssop-water, and this they gave him to drink when he was thirsty; a drop of water would have cooled his tongue better than a draught of vinegar: yet this he submitted to for us. <hi type="italic">We had taken the sour grapes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">thus his teeth were set on edge;</hi> we had forfeited all comforts and refreshments, and therefore they were withheld from him. When heaven denied him a beam of light earth denied him a drop of water, and put vinegar in the room of it. <div eID="gen28609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28610" type="x-p"/> V. The dying word wherewith he breathed out his soul (<reference osisRef="John.19.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had received the vinegar,</hi> as much of it as he thought fit, <hi type="italic">he said, It is finished;</hi> and, with that, <hi type="italic">bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28611" type="x-p"/> 1. What he said, and we may suppose him to say it with triumph and exultation, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Tetelestai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> a comprehensive word, and a comfortable one. (1.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the malice and enmity of his persecutors had now done their worst; <hi type="italic">when he had received</hi> that last indignity in <hi type="italic">the vinegar they gave him, he said,</hi> "This is the last; I am now going out of their reach, <hi type="italic">where the wicked cease from troubling.</hi>" (2.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the counsel and commandment of his Father concerning his sufferings were now fulfilled; it was a <hi type="italic">determinate counsel,</hi> and he took care to see every iota and tittle of it exactly answered, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. He had said, when he entered upon his sufferings, <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done;</hi> and now he saith with pleasure, <hi type="italic">It is done.</hi> It was <hi type="italic">his meat and drink to finish his work</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.34">ch. iv. 34</reference>), and the meat and drink refreshed him, when they gave him gall and vinegar. (3.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, all the types and prophecies of the Old Testament, which pointed at the sufferings of the Messiah, were accomplished and answered. He speaks as if, now that <hi type="italic">they had given him the vinegar,</hi> he could not bethink himself of any word in the Old Testament that was to be fulfilled between him and his death but it had its accomplishment; such as, his being <hi type="italic">sold for thirty pieces of silver, his hands and feet being pierced, his garments divided, &c.;</hi> and now that this is done. <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> (4.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the ceremonial law is abolished, and a period put to the obligation of it. The substance is now come, and all the shadows are done away. Just now <hi type="italic">the veil is rent, the wall of partition is taken down,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the law of commandments contained in ordinances,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 14, 15</reference>. The Mosaic economy is dissolved, <hi type="italic">to make way for a better hope.</hi> (5.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, sin is finished, and an end made of transgression, by <hi type="italic">the bringing in of an everlasting righteousness.</hi> It seems to refer to <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lamb of God was sacrificed to take away the sin of the world,</hi> and it is done, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 26</reference>. (6.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, his sufferings were now finished, both those of his soul and those of his body. The storm is over, the worst is past; all his pains and agonies are at an end, and he is just going to paradise, entering upon <hi type="italic">the joy set before him.</hi> Let all that <hi type="italic">suffer for Christ,</hi> and with Christ, comfort themselves with this, <hi type="italic">that yet a little while</hi> and they also shall say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> (7.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, his life was now finished, he was just ready to breathe his last, and <hi type="italic">now he is no more in this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.11">ch. xvii. 11</reference>. This is like that of blessed Paul (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2 Tim. iv. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have finished my course,</hi> my race is run, my glass is out, <hi type="italic">mene, mene—numbered</hi> and <hi type="italic">finished.</hi> This we must all come to shortly. (8.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the work of man's redemption and salvation is now completed, at least the hardest part of the undertaking is over; a full satisfaction is made to the justice of God, a fatal blow given to the power of Satan, a fountain of grace opened that shall ever flow, a foundation of peace and happiness laid that shall never fail. Christ had now gone through with his work, and <hi type="italic">finished it,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.4">ch. xvii. 4</reference>. For, <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect; when I begin,</hi> saith he, <hi type="italic">I will also make an end.</hi> And, as in the purchase, so in the application of the redemption, <hi type="italic">he that has begun a good work will perform it;</hi> the mystery of God shall be finished. <div eID="gen28611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28612" type="x-p"/> 2. What he did: <hi type="italic">He bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.</hi> He was voluntary in dying; for he was not only the sacrifice, but the priest and the offerer; and the <hi type="italic">animus offerentis—the mind of the offerer,</hi> was all in all in the sacrifice. Christ showed his will in his sufferings, <hi type="italic">by which will we are sanctified.</hi> (1.) <hi type="italic">He gave up the ghost.</hi> His life was not forcibly extorted from him, but freely resigned. He had said, <hi type="italic">Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit,</hi> thereby expressing the intention of this act. I give up myself as a <hi type="italic">ransom for many;</hi> and, accordingly, he did give up his spirit, paid down the price of pardon and life at his Father's hands. <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">He bowed his head.</hi> Those that were crucified, in dying stretched up their heads to gasp for breath, and did not drop their heads till they had breathed their last; but Christ, to show himself active in dying, <hi type="italic">bowed his head</hi> first, composing himself, as it were, to fall asleep. God <hi type="italic">had laid upon him the iniquity of us all,</hi> putting it upon the head of this great sacrifice; and some think that by this bowing of his head he would intimate his sense of the weight upon him. See <reference osisRef="Ps.38.4">Ps. xxxviii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">xl. 12</reference>. The bowing of his head shows his submission to his Father's will, and his obedience to death. He accommodated himself to his dying work, as Jacob, <hi type="italic">who gathered up his feet into the bed, and then yielded up the ghost.</hi>
entries.8076c43c727eb32c4f09c71be3307a2428684990: <div eID="gen28612" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen28613" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was a high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they might be taken away. <hi type="super">32</hi> Then came the soldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him. <hi type="super">33</hi> But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs: <hi type="super">34</hi> But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water. <hi type="super">35</hi> And he that saw <hi type="italic">it</hi> bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe. <hi type="super">36</hi> For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken. <hi type="super">37</hi> And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced. <div eID="gen28613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28614" type="x-p"/> This passage concerning the piercing of Christ's side after his death is recorded only by this evangelist. <div eID="gen28614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28615" type="x-p"/> I. Observe the superstition of the Jews, which occasioned it (<reference osisRef="John.19.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because it was the preparation for the sabbath, and that sabbath day,</hi> because it fell in the passover-week, <hi type="italic">was a high day,</hi> that they might show a veneration for the sabbath, they would <hi type="italic">not have the dead bodies to remain on the crosses on the sabbath-day,</hi> but <hi type="italic">besought Pilate that their legs might be broken,</hi> which would be a certain, but cruel dispatch, and that then they might be buried out of sight. Note here, 1. The esteem they would be thought to have for the approaching sabbath, because it was one of the days of unleavened bread, and (some reckon) the day of the offering of the first-fruits. Every sabbath day is a holy day, and a good day, but this was a high day, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">megale hemera</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a great day.</hi> Passover sabbaths are high days; sacrament-days, supper-days, communion-days are high days, and there ought to be more than ordinary preparation for them, that these may be high days indeed to us, <hi type="italic">as the days of heaven.</hi> 2. The reproach which they reckoned it would be to that day if the dead bodies should be left hanging on the crosses. Dead bodies were not to be left at any time (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">Deut. xxi. 23</reference>); yet, in this case, the Jews would have left the Roman custom to take place, had it not been an extraordinary day; and, many strangers from all parts being then at Jerusalem, it would have been an offence to them; nor could they well bear the sight of Christ's crucified body, for, unless their consciences were quite seared, when the heat of their rage was a little over, they would upbraid them. 3. Their petition to Pilate, that their bodies, now as good as dead, might be dispatched; not by strangling or beheading them, which would have been a compassionate hastening of them out of their misery, like the <hi type="italic">coup de grace</hi> (as the French call it) to those that are broken upon the wheel, <hi type="italic">the stroke of mercy,</hi> but by the breaking of their legs, which would carry them off in the most exquisite pain. Note, (1.) <hi type="italic">The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.</hi> (2.) The pretended sanctity of hypocrites is abominable. These Jews would be thought to bear a great regard for the sabbath, and yet had not regard to justice and righteousness; they made no conscience of bringing an innocent and excellent person to the cross, and yet scrupled letting a dead body hang upon the cross. <div eID="gen28615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28616" type="x-p"/> II. The dispatching of <hi type="italic">the two thieves that were crucified with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.32">v. 32</reference>. Pilate was still gratifying the Jews, and gave orders as they desired; <hi type="italic">and the soldiers came,</hi> hardened against all impressions of pity, <hi type="italic">and broke the legs of the two thieves,</hi> which, no doubt, extorted from them hideous outcries, and made them die according to the bloody disposition of Nero, so as to feel themselves die. One of these thieves was a penitent, and had received from Christ an assurance that he should shortly be with him in paradise, and yet died in the same pain and misery that the other thief did; for <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all.</hi> Many go to heaven that <hi type="italic">have bands in their death,</hi> and <hi type="italic">die in the bitterness of their soul.</hi> The extremity of dying agonies is no obstruction to the living comforts that wait for holy souls on the other side death. Christ died, and went to paradise, but appointed a guard to convey him thither. This is the order of going to heaven—<hi type="italic">Christ, the first-fruits</hi> and forerunner, <hi type="italic">afterwards those that are Christ's.</hi> <div eID="gen28616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28617" type="x-p"/> III. The trial that was made whether Christ was dead or no, and the putting of it out of doubt. <div eID="gen28617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28618" type="x-p"/> 1. They supposed him to be dead, and therefore <hi type="italic">did not break his legs,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.33">v. 33</reference>. Observe here, (1.) That Jesus died in less time than persons crucified ordinarily did. The structure of his body, perhaps, being extraordinarily fine and tender, was the sooner broken by pain; or, rather, it was to show that he laid down his life of himself, and could die when he pleased, though his hands were nailed. Though he yielded to death, yet he was not conquered. (2.) That his enemies were satisfied he was really dead. The Jews, who stood by to see the execution effectually done, would not have omitted this piece of cruelty, if they had not been sure he was got out of the reach of it. (3.) <hi type="italic">Whatever devices are in men's hearts, the counsel of the Lord shall stand.</hi> It was fully designed to break his legs, but, God's counsel being otherwise, see how it was prevented. <div eID="gen28618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28619" type="x-p"/> 2. Because they would be sure he was dead they made such an experiment as would put it past dispute. <hi type="italic">One of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side,</hi> aiming at his heart, <hi type="italic">and forthwith came there out blood and water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.34">v. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen28619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28620" type="x-p"/> (1.) The soldier hereby designed to decide the question whether he was dead or no, and by this honourable wound in his side to supersede the ignominious method of dispatch they took with the other two. Tradition says that this soldier's name was <hi type="italic">Longinus,</hi> and that, having some distemper in his eyes, he was immediately cured of it, by some drops of blood that flowed out of Christ's side falling on them: significant enough, if we had any good authority for the story. <div eID="gen28620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28621" type="x-p"/> (2.) But God had a further design herein, which was, <div eID="gen28621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28622" type="x-p"/> [1.] To give an evidence of the truth of his death, in order to the proof of his resurrection. If he was only in a trance or swoon, his resurrection was a sham; but, by this experiment, he was certainly dead, for this spear broke up the very fountains of life, and, according to all the law and course of nature, it was impossible a human body should survive such a wound as this in the vitals, and such an evacuation thence. <div eID="gen28622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28623" type="x-p"/> [2.] To give an illustration of the design of his death. There was much of mystery in it, and its being solemnly attested (<reference osisRef="John.19.35">v. 35</reference>) intimates there was something miraculous in it, that <hi type="italic">the blood and water</hi> should come out distinct and separate from the same wound; at least it was very significant; this same apostle refers to it as a very considerable thing, <reference osisRef="1John.5.6">1 John v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen28623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the opening of his side was significant. When we would protest our sincerity, we wish there were a window in our hearts, that the thoughts and intents of them might be visible to all. Through this window, opened in Christ's side, you may look into his heart, and see love flaming there, love strong as death; see our names written there. Some make it an allusion to the opening of Adam's side in innocency. When Christ, the second Adam, was fallen into a deep sleep upon the cross, then was his side opened, and out of it was his church taken, which he espoused to himself. See <reference osisRef="Eph.5.30">Eph. v. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">32</reference>. Our devout poet, Mr. George Herbert, in his poem called <hi type="italic">The Bag,</hi> very affectingly brings in our Saviour, when his side was pierced, thus speaking to his disciples:— <div eID="gen28624" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen28625"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28626"/>If ye have any thing to send, or write<l eID="gen28626" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28627"/>(I have no bag, but here is room),<l eID="gen28627" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28628"/>Unto my Father's hands and sight<l eID="gen28628" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28629"/>(Believe me) it shall safely come.<l eID="gen28629" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28630"/>That I shall mind what you impart,<l eID="gen28630" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28631"/>Look, you may put it very near my heart;<l eID="gen28631" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28632"/>Or, if hereafter any of my friends<l eID="gen28632" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28633"/>Will use me in this kind, the door<l eID="gen28633" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28634"/>Shall still be open; what he sends<l eID="gen28634" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28635"/>I will present, and somewhat more,<l eID="gen28635" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28636"/>Not to his hurt. Sighs will convey<l eID="gen28636" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28637"/>Any thing to me. Hark, Despair, away.<l eID="gen28637" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen28625"/> <div sID="gen28638" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, The blood and water</hi> that flowed out of it were significant. 1. They signified the two great benefits which all believers partake of through Christ-justification and sanctification; blood for remission, water for regeneration; blood for atonement, water for purification. Blood and water were used very much under the law. Guilt contracted must be expiated by blood; stains contracted must be done away by <hi type="italic">the water of purification.</hi> These two must always go together. <hi type="italic">You are sanctified, you are justified,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. Christ has joined them together, and we must not think to put them asunder. They both flowed from the pierced side of our Redeemer. To Christ crucified we owe both merit for our justification, and Spirit and grace for our sanctification; and we have as much need of the latter as of the former, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1 Cor. i. 30</reference>. 2. They signified the two great ordinances of baptism and the Lord's supper, by which those benefits are represented, sealed, and applied, to believers; they both owe their institution and efficacy to Christ. It is not the water in the font that will be to us <hi type="italic">the washing of regeneration,</hi> but the water out of the side of Christ; not the blood of the grape that will pacify the conscience and refresh the soul, but the blood out of the side of Christ. Now was the rock smitten (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1 Cor. x. 4</reference>), now was the fountain opened (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zech. xiii. 1</reference>), now were the wells of salvation digged, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa. xii. 3</reference>. Here <hi type="italic">is the river, the streams whereof make glad the city of our God.</hi> <div eID="gen28638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28639" type="x-p"/> IV. The attestation of the truth of this by an eye-witness (<reference osisRef="John.19.35">v. 35</reference>), the evangelist himself. Observe, <div eID="gen28639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28640" type="x-p"/> 1. What a competent witness he was of the matters of fact. (1.) What he bore record of he saw; he had it not by hearsay, nor was it only his own conjecture, but he was an eyewitness of it; it is <hi type="italic">what we have seen and looked upon</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Jo.1.1 2Pe 1.16">1 John i. 1; 2 Pet. i. 16</reference>), and <hi type="italic">had perfect understanding of,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Luke i. 3</reference>. (2.) What he saw he faithfully bore record of; as a faithful witness, he told not only the truth, but the whole truth; and did not only attest it by word of mouth, but left it upon record in writing, <hi type="italic">in perpetuam rei memoriam—for a perpetual memorial.</hi> (3.) <hi type="italic">His record is</hi> undoubtedly <hi type="italic">true;</hi> for he wrote not only from his own personal knowledge and observation, but from the dictates of the Spirit of truth, that leads into all truth. (4.) He had himself a full assurance of the truth of what he wrote, and did not persuade others to believe that which he did not believe himself: <hi type="italic">He knows that he saith true.</hi> (5.) He <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> witnessed these things, <hi type="italic">that we might believe;</hi> he did not record them merely for his own satisfaction or the private use of his friends, but made them public to the world; not to please the curious nor entertain the ingenious, but to draw men to believe the gospel in order to their eternal welfare. <div eID="gen28640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28641" type="x-p"/> 2. What care he showed in this particular instance. That we may be well assured of the truth of Christ's death, he saw his heart's blood, his life's blood, let out; and also of the benefits that flow to us from his death, signified by the blood and water which came out of his side. Let this silence the fears of weak Christians, and encourage their hopes, <hi type="italic">iniquity shall not be their ruin,</hi> for there came both water and blood out of Christ's pierced side, both to justify and sanctify them; and if you ask, How can we be sure of this? You may be sure, for <hi type="italic">he that saw it bore record.</hi> <div eID="gen28641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28642" type="x-p"/> V. The accomplishment of the scripture in all this (<reference osisRef="John.19.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the scripture might be fulfilled,</hi> and so both the honour of the Old Testament preserved and the truth of the New Testament confirmed. Here are two instances of it together:— <div eID="gen28642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28643" type="x-p"/> 1. The scripture was fulfilled in the preserving of his legs from being broken; therein that word was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">A bone of him shall not be broken.</hi> (1.) There was a promise of this made indeed to all <hi type="italic">the righteous,</hi> but principally pointing at <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ the righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.20">Ps. xxxiv. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He keepeth all his bones, not one of them is broken.</hi> And David, in spirit, says, <hi type="italic">All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.35.10">Ps. xxxv. 10</reference>. (2.) There was a type of this in the paschal lamb, which seems to be specially referred to here (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.46">Exod. xii. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Neither shall you break a bone thereof;</hi> and it is repeated (<reference osisRef="Num.9.12">Num. ix. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">You shall not break any bone of it;</hi> for which law the will of the law-maker is the reason, but the antitype must answer the type. <hi type="italic">Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">the Lamb of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">ch. i. 29</reference>), and, as the true passover, his bones were kept unbroken. This commandment was given concerning his bones, when dead, as of Joseph's, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.22">Heb. xi. 22</reference>. (3.) There was a significancy in it; the strength of the body is in the bones. The Hebrew word for the bones signifies the strength, and therefore <hi type="italic">not a bone of Christ must be broken,</hi> to show that though <hi type="italic">he be crucified in weakness</hi> his strength to save is not at all broken. Sin breaks our bones, as it broke David's (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Ps. li. 8</reference>); but it did not break Christ's bones; he stood firm under the burden, mighty to save. <div eID="gen28643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28644" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The scripture was fulfilled in the piercing of his side</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.19.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall look on me whom they had pierced;</hi> so it is written, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>. And there the same that pours out the Spirit of grace, and can be no less than the God of the holy prophets, says, <hi type="italic">They shall look upon me,</hi> which is here applied to Christ, <hi type="italic">They shall look upon him.</hi> (1.) It is here implied that the Messiah shall be pierced; and here it had a more full accomplishment than in <hi type="italic">the piercing of his hands and feet;</hi> he was pierced by <hi type="italic">the house of David</hi> and <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Jerusalem, wounded in the house of his friends,</hi> as it follows, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.6">Zech. xiii. 6</reference>. (2.) It is promised that <hi type="italic">when the Spirit is poured out they shall look on him and mourn.</hi> This was in part fulfilled when many of those that were his betrayers and murderers <hi type="italic">were pricked to the heart,</hi> and brought to believe in him; it will be further fulfilled, in mercy, <hi type="italic">when all Israel shall be saved;</hi> and, in wrath, when those who persisted in their infidelity shall <hi type="italic">see him whom they have pierced, and wail because of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>. But it is applicable to us all. We have all been guilty of piercing the Lord Jesus, and are all concerned with suitable affections to look on him.
entries.ec959614b5bcb8b67a69af1660c084941fea95a6: <div eID="gen28644" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burial of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen28645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> And after this Joseph of Arimathæa, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave <hi type="italic">him</hi> leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus. 39 And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pound <hi type="italic">weight.</hi> <hi type="super">40</hi> Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury. <hi type="super">41</hi> Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid. <hi type="super">42</hi> There laid they Jesus therefore because of the Jews' preparation <hi type="italic">day;</hi> for the sepulchre was nigh at hand. <div eID="gen28645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28646" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the burial of the blessed body of our Lord Jesus. The solemn funerals of great men are usually looked at with curiosity; the mournful funerals of dear friends are attended with concern. Come and see an extraordinary funeral; never was the like! Come and see a burial that conquered the grave, and buried it, a burial that beautified the grave and softened it for all believers. <hi type="italic">Let us turn aside now, and see this great sight.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen28646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28647" type="x-p"/> I. The body begged, <reference osisRef="John.19.38">v. 38</reference>. This was done by the interest of <hi type="italic">Joseph of Ramah,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Arimathea,</hi> of whom no mention is made in all the New-Testament story, but only in the narrative which each of the evangelists gives us of Christ's burial, wherein he was chiefly concerned. Observe, 1. The character of this Joseph. He was a disciple of Christ <hi type="italic">incognito—in secret,</hi> a better friend to Christ than he would willingly be known to be. It was his honour that he was a disciple of Christ; and some such there are, that are themselves great men, and unavoidably linked with bad men. But it was his weakness that he was so secretly, when he should have confessed Christ before men, yea, though he had lost his preferment by it. Disciples should openly own themselves, yet Christ may have many that are his disciples sincerely, though secretly; better secretly than not at all, especially if, like Joseph here, they grow stronger and stronger. Some who in less trials have been timorous, yet in greater have been very courageous; so Joseph here. He concealed his affection to Christ <hi type="italic">for fear of the Jews,</hi> lest they should put him out of the synagogue, at least out of the sanhedrim, which was all they could do. To Pilate the governor he <hi type="italic">went boldly,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">feared the Jews.</hi> The impotent malice of those that can but censure, and revile, and clamour, is sometimes more formidable even to wise and good men than one would think. 2. The part he bore in this affair. He, having by his place access to Pilate, desired leave of him to dispose of the body. His mother and dear relations had neither spirit nor interest to attempt such a thing. His disciples were gone; if nobody appeared, the Jews or soldiers would bury him with the thieves; therefore God raised up this gentleman to interpose in it, that the scripture might be fulfilled, and the decorum owing to his approaching resurrection maintained. Note, When God has work to do he can find out such as are proper to do it, and embolden them for it. Observe it as an instance of the humiliation of Christ, that his dead body lay at the mercy of a heathen judge, and must be begged before it could be buried, and also that Joseph would not take the body of Christ till he had asked and obtained leave of the governor; for in those things wherein the power of the magistrate is concerned we must ever pay a deference to that power, and peaceably submit to it. <div eID="gen28647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28648" type="x-p"/> II. The embalming prepared, <reference osisRef="John.19.39">v. 39</reference>. This was done by Nicodemus, another person of quality, and in a public post. He brought a <hi type="italic">mixture of myrrh and aloes,</hi> which some think were bitter ingredients, to preserve the body, others fragrant ones, to perfume it. Here is. 1. The character of Nicodemus, which is much the same with that of Joseph; he was a secret friend to Christ, though not his constant follower. He at first <hi type="italic">came to Jesus by night,</hi> but now owned him publicly, as before, <reference osisRef="John.7.50-John.7.51">ch. vii. 50, 51</reference>. That grace which at first is like a bruised reed may afterwards become like a strong cedar, and the trembling lamb <hi type="italic">bold as a lion.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.14.4">Rom. xiv. 4</reference>. It is a wonder that Joseph and Nicodemus, men of such interest, did not appear sooner, and solicit Pilate not to condemn Christ, especially seeing him so loth to do it. Begging his life would have been a nobler piece of service than begging his body. But Christ would have none of his friends to endeavour to prevent his death when his hour was come. While his persecutors were forwarding the accomplishment of the scriptures, his followers must not obstruct it. 2. The kindness of Nicodemus, which was considerable, though of a different nature. Joseph served Christ with his interest, Nicodemus with his purse. Probably, they agreed it between them, that, while one was procuring the grant, the other should be preparing the spices; and this for expedition, because they were straitened in time. But why did they make this ado about Christ's dead body? (1.) Some think we may see in it the weakness of their faith. A firm belief of the resurrection of Christ on the third day would have saved them this care and cost, and have been more acceptable than all spices. Those bodies indeed to whom the grave is a long home need to be clad accordingly; but what need of such furniture of the grave for one that, like a way-faring man, did but turn aside into it, to <hi type="italic">tarry for a night or two?</hi> (2.) However, we may plainly see in it the strength of their love. Hereby they showed the value they had for his person and doctrine, and that it was not lessened by the reproach of the cross. Those that had been so industrious to profane his crown, and lay his honour in the dust, might already see that they had imagined a vain thing; for, as God had done him honour in his sufferings, so did men too, even great men. They showed not only the charitable respect of committing his body to the earth, but the honourable respect shown to great men. This they might do, and yet believe and look for his resurrection; nay, this they might do in the belief and expectation of it. Since God designed honour for this body, they would put honour upon it. However, we must do our duty according as the present day and opportunity are, and leave it to God to fulfil his promises in his own way and time. <div eID="gen28648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28649" type="x-p"/> III. The body got ready, <reference osisRef="John.19.40">v. 40</reference>. They <hi type="italic">took it</hi> into some house adjoining, and, having washed it from blood and dust, <hi type="italic">wound it in linen clothes</hi> very decently, with the spices melted down, it is likely, into an ointment, as <hi type="italic">the manner of the Jews is to bury,</hi> or to <hi type="italic">embalm</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), as we sear dead bodies. 1. Here was care taken of Christ's body: It was <hi type="italic">wound in linen clothes.</hi> Among clothing that belongs to us, Christ put on even the grave-clothes, to make them easy to us, and to enable us to call them our wedding-clothes. They wound the body <hi type="italic">with the spices,</hi> for <hi type="italic">all his garments,</hi> his grave-clothes not excepted, <hi type="italic">smell of myrrh and aloes</hi> (the spices here mentioned) <hi type="italic">out of the ivory palaces</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Ps. xlv. 8</reference>), and an ivory palace the sepulchre hewn out of a rock was to Christ. Dead bodies and graves are noisome and offensive; hence sin is compared to a <hi type="italic">body of death</hi> and an <hi type="italic">open sepulchre;</hi> but Christ's sacrifice, being to God as a sweet-smelling savour, hath taken away our pollution. No ointment or perfume can rejoice the heart so as the grave of our Redeemer does, where there is faith to perceive the fragrant odours of it. 2. In conformity to this example, we ought to have regard to the dead bodies of Christians; not to enshrine and adore their relics, no, not those of the most eminent saints and martyrs (nothing like that was done to the dead body of Christ himself), but carefully to deposit them, the dust in the dust, as those who believe that the dead bodies of the saints are still united to Christ and designed for glory and immortality at the last day. The resurrection of the saints will be in virtue of Christ's resurrection, and therefore in burying them we should have an eye to Christ's burial, for he, being dead, thus speaketh. <hi type="italic">Thy dead men shall live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. In burying our dead it is not necessary that in all circumstances we imitate the burial of Christ, as if we must be buried in linen, and in a garden, and be embalmed as he was; but his being buried after <hi type="italic">the manner of the Jews</hi> teaches us that in things of this nature we should conform to the usages of the country where we live, except in those that are superstitious. <div eID="gen28649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28650" type="x-p"/> IV. The grave pitched upon, in a garden which belonged to Joseph of Arimathea, very near the place where he was crucified. There was a sepulchre, or vault, prepared for the first occasion, but not yet used. Observe, <div eID="gen28650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28651" type="x-p"/> 1. That Christ was buried without the city, for thus the manner of the Jews was to bury, not in their cities, much less in their synagogues, which some have thought better than our way of burying: yet there was then a peculiar reason for it, which does not hold now, because the touching of a grave contracted a ceremonial pollution: but now that the resurrection of Christ has altered the property of the grave, and done away its pollution for all believers, we need not keep at such a distance from it; nor is it incapable of a good improvement, to have the congregation of the dead in the church-yard, encompassing the congregation of the living in the church, since they also are dying, and in <hi type="italic">the midst of life we are in death.</hi> Those that would not superstitiously, but by faith, visit the holy sepulchre, must go forth out of the noise of this world. <div eID="gen28651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28652" type="x-p"/> 2. That Christ was buried in a garden. Observe, (1.) That Joseph had his sepulchre in his garden; so he contrived it, that it might be a memento, [1.] To himself while living; when he was taking the pleasure of his garden, and reaping the products of it, let him think of dying, and be quickened to prepare for it. The garden is a proper place for meditation, and a sepulchre there may furnish us with a proper subject for meditation, and such a one as we are loth to admit in the midst of our pleasures. [2.] To his heirs and successors when he was gone. It is good to acquaint ourselves with the <hi type="italic">place of our fathers' sepulchres;</hi> and perhaps we might make our own less formidable if we made theirs more familiar. (2.) That in a sepulchre in a garden Christ's body was laid. In the garden of Eden death and the grave first received their power, and now in a garden they are conquered, disarmed, and triumphed over. In a garden Christ began his passion, and from a garden he would rise, and begin his exaltation. Christ fell to the ground <hi type="italic">as a corn of wheat</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.24">ch. xii. 24</reference>), and therefore was sown in a garden among the seeds, for <hi type="italic">his dew is as the dew of herbs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. He is the <hi type="italic">fountain of gardens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.15">Cant. iv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen28652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28653" type="x-p"/> 3. That he was buried in a new sepulchre. This was so ordered (1.) For the honour of Christ; he was not a common person, and therefore must not mix with common dust He that was born from a virgin-womb must rise from a virgin-tomb. (2.) For the confirming of the truth of his resurrection, that it might not be suggested that it was not he, but some other that rose now, when many bodies of saints arose; or, that he rose by the power of some other, as the man that was raised by the touch of Elisha's bones, and not by his own power. He that has <hi type="italic">made all things new</hi> has new-made the grave for us. <div eID="gen28653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28654" type="x-p"/> V. The funeral solemnized (<reference osisRef="John.19.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">There laid they Jesus,</hi> that is, the dead body of Jesus. Some think the calling of this <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> intimates the inseparable union between the divine and human nature. Even this dead body was <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour,</hi> for his death is our life; Jesus is still the same, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">Heb. xiii. 8</reference>. There they laid him because it was the preparation day. <div eID="gen28654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28655" type="x-p"/> 1. Observe here the deference which the Jews paid to the sabbath, and to the day of preparation. Before the passover-sabbath they had a solemn day of preparation. This day had been ill kept by the chief priests, who called themselves the church, but was well kept by the disciples of Christ, who were branded as dangerous to the church; and it is often so. (1.) They would not put off the funeral till the sabbath day, because the sabbath is to be a day of holy rest and joy, with which the business and sorrow of a funeral do not well agree. (2.) They would not drive it too late on the day of preparation for the sabbath. What is to be done the evening before the sabbath should be so contrived that it may neither intrench upon sabbath time, nor indispose us for sabbath work. <div eID="gen28655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28656" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe the convenience they took of an adjoining sepulchre; the sepulchre they made use of was <hi type="italic">nigh at hand.</hi> Perhaps, if they had had time, they would have carried him to Bethany, and buried him among his friends there. And I am sure he had more right to have been buried in the chief of the sepulchres of the sons of David than any of the kings of Judah had; but it was so ordered that he should be laid in a sepulchre nigh at hand, (1.) Because he was to lie there but awhile, as in an inn, and therefore he took the first that offered itself. (2.) Because this was a new sepulchre. Those that prepared it little thought who should handsel it; but the wisdom of God has reaches infinitely beyond ours, and he makes what use he pleases of us and all we have. (3.) We are hereby taught not to be over-curious in the place of our burial. Where the tree falls, why should it not lie? For Christ was buried in the sepulchre that was next at hand. It was faith in the promise of Canaan that directed the Patriarch's desires to be carried thither for a burying-place; but now, since that promise is superseded by a better, that care is over. <div eID="gen28656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28657" type="x-p"/> Thus without pomp or solemnity is the body of Jesus laid in the cold and silent grave. Here lies our surety under arrest for our debts, so that if he be released his discharge will be ours. Here is the Sun of righteousness set for awhile, to rise again in greater glory, and set no more. Here lies a seeming captive to death, but a real conqueror over death; for here lies death itself slain, and the grave conquered. <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.19"/> <div eID="gen28657" type="x-p"/>

entries.b86666465334c1dc7f164e21b1c256f6f1af9663: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15444"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.19.1-John.19.16">Joh 19:1-16</reference>. Jesus before Pilate--Scourged--Treated with Other Severities and Insults--Delivered Up, and Led Away to Be Crucified.</title> <div sID="gen29741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15444"/><hi type="bold">1-3. Pilate took Jesus and scourged him--</hi>in hope of appeasing them. (See <reference osisRef="Mark.15.15">Mr 15:15</reference>). "And the soldiers led Him away into the palace, and they call the whole band" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.16">Mr 15:16</reference>)--the body of the military cohort stationed there--to take part in the mock coronation now to be enacted. <div eID="gen29741" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e00a53b067d0a8be25a5b01dece58d29cb39aa3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15447"/><div sID="gen29745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15447"/><hi type="bold">4-5. Pilate ... went forth again, and saith ... Behold, I bring him forth to you--</hi>am bringing, that is, going to bring him forth to you.<div eID="gen29745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye may know I find no fault in him--</hi>and, by scourging Him and allowing the soldiers to make sport of Him, have gone as far to meet your exasperation as can be expected from a judge. <div eID="gen29746" type="x-p"/>
entries.b80c607458554ac7eca8ad01f4cbe60db6891b02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15449"/><div sID="gen29748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15449"/><hi type="bold">6-7. When the chief priests ... saw him, they cried out--</hi>their fiendish rage kindling afresh at the sight of Him.<div eID="gen29748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Crucify him, crucify him--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Mark.15.14">Mr 15:14</reference>).<div eID="gen29749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pilate saith unto them, Take ye him, and crucify him; for I find no fault in him--</hi>as if this would relieve him of the responsibility of the deed, who, by surrendering Him, incurred it all! <div eID="gen29750" type="x-p"/>
entries.b42247decdcedc92b147993c118461cdb2e4ebbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15451"/><div sID="gen29752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15451"/><hi type="bold">8-11. When Pilate ... heard this saying, he was the more afraid--</hi>the name "Son of God," the lofty sense evidently attached to it by His Jewish accusers, the dialogue he had already held with Him, and the dream of his wife (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.19">Mt 27:19</reference>), all working together in the breast of the wretched man. <div eID="gen29752" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e55e6e85d42c704919a3dd710ecb2cb546946bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15455"/><div sID="gen29763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15455"/><hi type="bold">12-16. And from thenceforth--</hi>particularly this speech, which seems to have filled him with awe, and redoubled his anxiety.<div eID="gen29763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pilate sought to release him--</hi>that is, to gain their consent to it, for he could have done it at once on his authority.<div eID="gen29764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the Jews cried--</hi>seeing their advantage, and not slow to profit by it. If thou let this man go, thou art not Cæsar's friend, &c.--"This was equivalent to a threat of impeachment, which we know was much dreaded by such officers as the procurators, especially of the character of Pilate or Felix. It also consummates the treachery and disgrace of the Jewish rulers, who were willing, for the purpose of destroying Jesus, to affect a zeal for the supremacy of a foreign prince" [Webster and Wilkinson]. (See <reference osisRef="John.19.15">Joh 19:15</reference>).<div eID="gen29765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">When Pilate ... heard that, ... he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in--</hi>"upon"<div eID="gen29766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the judgment seat--</hi>that he might pronounce sentence against the Prisoner, on this charge, the more solemnly.<div eID="gen29767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a place called the Pavement--</hi>a tesselated pavement, much used by the Romans.<div eID="gen29768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Hebrew, Gabbatha--</hi>from its being raised. <div eID="gen29769" type="x-p"/>
entries.504e04af1ebf652c0d9a5dac65bec97eee4e5937: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15459"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.19.17-John.19.30">Joh 19:17-30</reference>. Crucifixion and Death of the Lord Jesus.</title> <div sID="gen29775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15459"/><hi type="bold">17. And he bearing his cross--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.23.26">Lu 23:26</reference>).<div eID="gen29775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went forth--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13">He 13:11-13</reference>, "without the camp"; "without the gate." On arriving at the place, "they gave Him vinegar to drink mingled with gall [wine mingled with myrrh, Mr 15:23], and when He had tasted thereof, He would not drink" (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.34">Mt 27:34</reference>). This potion was stupefying, and given to criminals just before execution, to deaden the sense of pain.<div eID="gen29776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29777" type="x-p"/> Fill high the bowl, and spice it well, and pour<div eID="gen29777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29778" type="x-p"/> The dews oblivious: for the Cross is sharp,<div eID="gen29778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29779" type="x-p"/> The Cross is sharp, and He<div eID="gen29779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29780" type="x-p"/> Is tenderer than a lamb.<div eID="gen29780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29781" type="x-p"/> Keble.<div eID="gen29781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29782" type="x-p"/> But our Lord would die with every faculty clear, and in full sensibility to all His sufferings.<div eID="gen29782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29783" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt feel all, that Thou may'st pity all;<div eID="gen29783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29784" type="x-p"/> And rather would'st Thou wrestle with strong pain<div eID="gen29784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29785" type="x-p"/> Than overcloud Thy soul,<div eID="gen29785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29786" type="x-p"/> So clear in agony,<div eID="gen29786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29787" type="x-p"/> Or lose one glimpse of Heaven before the time,<div eID="gen29787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29788" type="x-p"/> O most entire and perfect Sacrifice,<div eID="gen29788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29789" type="x-p"/> Renewed in every pulse.<div eID="gen29789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29790" type="x-p"/> Keble. <div eID="gen29790" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cda7c4bd0909f3b39125d58dc2a3161fa03b52f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15460"/><div sID="gen29791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15460"/><hi type="bold">18. they crucified him, and two others with him--</hi>"malefactors" (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.33">Lu 23:33</reference>), "thieves" (rather "robbers," <reference osisRef="Matt.27.38">Mt 27:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.15.27">Mr 15:27</reference>).<div eID="gen29791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on either side one and Jesus in the midst--</hi>a hellish expedient, to hold Him up as the worst of the three. But in this, as in many other of their doings, "the scripture was fulfilled, which saith (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>), And he was numbered with the transgressors"--(<reference osisRef="Mark.15.28">Mr 15:28</reference>)--though the prediction reaches deeper. "Then said Jesus"--["probably while being nailed to the Cross,"] [Olshausen], "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>)--and again the Scripture was fulfilled which said, "And He made intercession for the transgressors" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>), though this also reaches deeper. (See <reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Ac 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.27">13:27</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>). Often have we occasion to observe how our Lord is the first to fulfil His own precepts--thus furnishing the right interpretation and the perfect Model of them. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>). How quickly was it seen in "His martyr Stephen," that though He had left the earth in Person, His Spirit remained behind, and Himself could, in some of His brightest lineaments, be reproduced in His disciples! (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Ac 7:60</reference>). And what does the world in every age owe to these few words, spoken where and as they were spoken! <div eID="gen29792" type="x-p"/>
entries.27c88be831df177c8c6142d66ae10f1c3a70b665: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15461"/><div sID="gen29793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15461"/><hi type="bold">19-22. Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross ... Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews ... and it was written in Hebrew--</hi>or Syro-Chaldaic, the language of the country.<div eID="gen29793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Greek--</hi>the current language.<div eID="gen29794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Latin--</hi>the official language. These were the chief languages of the earth, and this secured that all spectators should be able to read it. Stung by this, the Jewish ecclesiastics entreat that it may be so altered as to express, not His real dignity, but His false claim to it. But Pilate thought he had yielded quite enough to them; and having intended expressly to spite and insult them by this title, for having got him to act against his own sense of justice, he peremptorily refused them. And thus, amidst the conflicting passions of men, was proclaimed, in the chief tongues of mankind, from the Cross itself and in circumstances which threw upon it a lurid yet grand light, the truth which drew the Magi to His manger, and will yet be owned by all the world! <div eID="gen29795" type="x-p"/>
entries.679e046993e957d26848fbdf85cc7c38df9a0ba4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15462"/><div sID="gen29796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15462"/><hi type="bold">23-24. Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts; to every soldier--</hi>the four who nailed Him to the cross, and whose perquisite they were.<div eID="gen29796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a part, and also his coat--</hi>the Roman tunic, or close-fitting vest.<div eID="gen29797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without seam, woven from the top throughout--</hi>"perhaps denoting considerable skill and labor as necessary to produce such a garment, the work probably of one or more of the women who ministered in such things unto Him, Lu 8:3" [Webster and Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen29798" type="x-p"/>
entries.716a9629f2761b8bf87bdca2ad95a08f15e75f97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15464"/><div sID="gen29800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15464"/><hi type="bold">25-27. Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary, wife of Cleophas--</hi>This should be read, as in the Margin, "Clopas," the same as "Alpheus" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.3">Mt 10:3</reference>). The "Cleopas" of <reference osisRef="Luke.24.18">Lu 24:18</reference> was a different person. <div eID="gen29800" type="x-p"/>
entries.394f4229d185cf8459c3a0486968a3e95c3c54e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15466"/><div sID="gen29803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15466"/><hi type="bold">28-30. After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished--</hi>that is, the moment for the fulfilment of the last of them; for there was one other small particular, and the time was come for that too, in consequence of the burning thirst which the fevered state of His frame occasioned (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Psa 22:15</reference>).<div eID="gen29803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the scripture--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">Psa 69:21</reference>).<div eID="gen29804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be fulfilled saith, I thirst. Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar--</hi>on the offer of the soldiers' vinegar, see on <reference osisRef="John.19.24">Joh 19:24</reference>.<div eID="gen29805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they--</hi>"one of them," (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.48">Mt 27:48</reference>). <div eID="gen29806" type="x-p"/>
entries.07b3037b8d53e53bfc015945bfda0377bc2aff5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15469"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.19.31-John.19.42">Joh 19:31-42</reference>. Burial of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen29810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15469"/><hi type="bold">31-37. the preparation--</hi>sabbath eve.<div eID="gen29810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the bodies should not remain--</hi>over night, against the Mosaic law (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.22">De 21:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen29811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the sabbath day, for that sabbath day was an high day--</hi>or "great" day--the first day of unleavened bread, and, as concurring with an ordinary sabbath, the most solemn season of the ecclesiastical year. Hence their peculiar jealousy lest the law should be infringed.<div eID="gen29812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">besought Pilate that their legs might be broken--</hi>to hasten their death, which was done in such cases with clubs. <div eID="gen29813" type="x-p"/>
entries.e36e95ab21400f3e9a98b8c6bdee30f23bb69a42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15475"/><div sID="gen29823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15475"/><hi type="bold">38-40. Joseph of Arimathea--</hi>"a rich man" (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.57">Mt 27:57</reference>), thus fulfilling <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Is 53:9</reference>; "an honorable counsellor," a member of the Sanhedrim, and of good condition, "which also waited for the kingdom of God" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.43">Mr 15:43</reference>), a devout expectant of Messiah's kingdom; "a good man and a just, the same had not consented to the counsel and deed of them" (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.50">Lu 23:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.51">51</reference>--he had gone the length, perhaps, of dissenting and protesting in open council against the condemnation of our Lord); "who also himself was Jesus' disciple," (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.57">Mt 27:57</reference>).<div eID="gen29823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews--</hi>"He went in boldly unto Pilate" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.43">Mr 15:43</reference>)--literally, "having taken courage went in," or "had the boldness to go in." Mark alone, as his manner is, notices the boldness which this required. The act would without doubt identify him for the first time with the disciples of Christ. Marvellous it certainly is, that one who while Jesus was yet alive merely refrained from condemning Him, not having the courage to espouse His cause by one positive act, should, now that He was dead, and His cause apparently dead with Him, summon up courage to go in personally to the Roman governor and ask permission to take down and inter the body. But if this be the first instance, it is not the last, that a seemingly dead Christ has wakened a sympathy which a living one had failed to evoke. The heroism of faith is usually kindled by desperate circumstances, and is not seldom displayed by those who before were the most timid, and scarce known as disciples at all. "And Pilate marvelled if he were already dead" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.44">Mr 15:44</reference>)--rather "wondered that he was already dead." "And calling the centurion, he asked him whether He had been any while dead" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.44">Mr 15:44</reference>)--Pilate could hardly credit what Joseph had told him, that He had been dead "some time," and, before giving up the body to His friends, would learn how the fact stood from the centurion, whose business it was to oversee the execution. "And when he knew it of the centurion" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.45">Mr 15:45</reference>), that it was as Joseph had said, "he gave"--rather "made a gift of"--"the body to Joseph"; struck, possibly, with the rank of the petitioner and the dignified boldness of the petition, in contrast with the spirit of the other party and the low rank to which he had been led to believe all the followers of Christ belonged. Nor would he be unwilling to Show that he was not going to carry this black affair any farther. But, whatever were Pilate's motives, two most blessed objects were thus secured: (1) The reality of our Lords death was attested by the party of all others most competent to decide on it, and certainly free from all bias--the officer in attendance--in full reliance on whose testimony Pilate surrendered the body: (2) The dead Redeemer, thus delivered out of the hands of His enemies, and committed by the supreme political authority to the care of His friends, was thereby protected from all further indignities; a thing most befitting indeed, now that His work was done, but impossible, so far as we can see, if His enemies had been at liberty to do with Him as they pleased. How wonderful are even the minutest features of this matchless History! <div eID="gen29824" type="x-p"/>
entries.167d63976f101cfe7c96e2ae39c94281a392075c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15478"/><div sID="gen29828" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15478"/><hi type="bold">41-42. Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new sepulchre--</hi>The choice of this tomb was, on their part, dictated by the double circumstance that it was so near at hand, and by its belonging to a friend of the Lord; and as there was need of haste, even they would be struck with the providence which thus supplied it. "There laid they Jesus therefore, because of the Jew's preparation day, for the sepulchre was nigh at hand." But there was one recommendation of it which probably would not strike them; but God had it in view. Not its being "hewn out of a rock" (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.46">Mr 15:46</reference>), accessible only at the entrance, which doubtless would impress them with its security and suitableness. But it was "a new sepulchre" (<reference osisRef="John.19.41">Joh 19:41</reference>), "wherein never man before was laid" (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.53">Lu 23:53</reference>): and Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.60">Mt 27:60</reference>) says that Joseph laid Him "in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock"--doubtless for his own use, though the Lord had higher use for it. Thus as He rode into Jerusalem on an ass "whereon never man before had sat" (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.2">Mr 11:2</reference>), so now He shall lie in a tomb wherein never man before had lain, that from these specimens it may be seen that in all things He was "SEPARATE FROM SINNERS" (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">He 7:26</reference>). <chapter eID="John.19"/>

entries.05e52c4870080caf062ee3b301451095401000a2: <div eID="gen42982" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen42983" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42984" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42984" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42983" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42985" type="x-p"/> Jesus is scourged, crowned with thorns, and mocked by the soldiers, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.1-Joh.19.3">Joh 19:1-3</reference>. He to brought forth by Pilate, wearing the purple robe; and the Jews clamor for his death, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.4-Joh.19.8">Joh 19:4-8</reference>. Conversation between our Lord and Pilate, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.9-Joh.19.11">Joh 19:9-11</reference>. Pilate expostulates with the Jews on their barbarous demands; but they become more inveterate, and he delivers Christ into their hands, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.12-Joh.19.16">Joh 19:12-16</reference>. He, bearing his cross, is led to Golgotha, and crucified, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.17-Joh.19.22">Joh 19:17-22</reference>. The soldiers cast lots for his raiment, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.23">Joh 19:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.24">Joh 19:24</reference>. Jesus commends his mother to the care of John, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.25-Joh.19.27">Joh 19:25-27</reference>. Jesus thirsts, receives vinegar, and dies, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.28-Joh.19.30">Joh 19:28-30</reference>. The Jews request that the legs of those who were crucified might be broken; the soldiers break those of the two thieves, and pierce the side of Christ; the Scriptures fulfilled in these acts, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.31-Joh.19.37">Joh 19:31-37</reference>. Joseph of Arimathea begs the body of Christ; and Nicodemus brings spices to embalm it, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.38-Joh.19.40">Joh 19:38-40</reference>. He is laid in a new sepulchre, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.41">Joh 19:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.42">Joh 19:42</reference>. <div eID="gen42985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42986" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen42986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42987" type="x-p"/> Pilate took Jesus, and scourged him - That is, caused him to be scourged: for we cannot with Bede suppose that he scourged him with his own hand. <div eID="gen42987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42988" type="x-p"/> As our Lord was scourged by order of Pilate, it is probable he was scourged in the Roman manner, which was much more severe than that of the Jews. The latter never gave more than thirty-nine blows; for the law had absolutely forbidden a man to be abused, or his flesh cut in this chastisement, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.3">Deu 25:3</reference>. The common method of whipping or flogging in some places, especially that of a military kind, is a disgrace to the nation where it is done, to the laws, and to humanity. See <reference osisRef="Mat.27.26">Mat 27:26</reference>, and the note there. Though it was customary to scourge the person who was to be crucified, yet it appears that Pilate had another end in view by scourging our Lord. He hoped that this would have satisfied the Jews, and that he might then have dismissed Jesus. This appears from <reference osisRef="Luk.23.16">Luk 23:16</reference>.
entries.2ca028083c2dbc8e1620eb53c8e074a133394e19: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen42988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42989" type="x-p"/> Platted a crown of thorns - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.29">Mat 27:29</reference> (note).
entries.87db5c08db48aa32d53c3c5f05d2803191a155ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen42989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42990" type="x-p"/> And Pilate saith - The word Pilate, which we supply in our version, is added by one MS., the later Syriac, later Arabic, and the Coptic. <div eID="gen42990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42991" type="x-p"/> Behold the man! - The man who, according to you, affects the government, and threatens to take away the empire from the Romans. Behold the man whom ye have brought unto me as an enemy to Caesar, and as a sower of the seeds of sedition in the land! In him I find no guilt; and from him ye have no occasion to fear any evil.
entries.597e26902ece52ef4f28af1451a0c9201cb73dce: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen42991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42992" type="x-p"/> Crucify Him - Αυτον, which is necessary to the text, and which is wanting in the common editions, and is supplied by our version in Italics, is added here on the authority of almost every MS. and version of importance. As it is omitted in the common editions, it affords another proof, that they were not taken from the best MSS.
entries.7f3b558e03ef6aba6dd1b3522446be6e9825497b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen42992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42993" type="x-p"/> We have a law - In <reference osisRef="Lev.24.14-Lev.24.16">Lev 24:14-16</reference>, we find that blasphemers of God were to be put to death; and the chief priests having charged Jesus with blasphemy, they therefore voted that he deserved to die. See <reference osisRef="Mat.26.65">Mat 26:65</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.66">Mat 26:66</reference>. They might refer also to the law against false prophets, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.20">Deu 18:20</reference>. <div eID="gen42993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42994" type="x-p"/> The Son of God - It is certain that the Jews understood this in a very peculiar sense. When Christ called himself the Son of God, they understood it to imply positive equality to the Supreme Being: and, if they were wrong, our Lord never attempted to correct them.
entries.9477ea65e0d476c02b82bf1ba2ef91b97bc80db4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen42994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42995" type="x-p"/> He was the more afraid - While Jesus was accused only as a disturber of the peace of the nation, which accusation Pilate knew to be false, he knew he could deliver him, because the judgment in that case belonged to himself; but when the Jews brought a charge against him of the most capital nature, from their own laws, he then saw that he had every thing to fear, if he did not deliver Jesus to their will. The Sanhedrin must not be offended - the populace must not be irritated: from the former a complaint might be sent against him to Caesar; the latter might revolt, or proceed to some acts of violence, the end of which could not be foreseen. Pilate was certainly to be pitied: he saw what was right, and he wished to do it; but he had not sufficient firmness of mind. He did not attend to that important maxim, Fiat justitia: ruat caelum. Let justice be done, though the heavens should be dissolved. He had a vile people to govern, and it was not an easy matter to keep them quiet. Some suppose that Pilate's fear arose from hearing that Jesus had said he was the Son of God; because Pilate, who was a polytheist, believed that it was possible for the offspring of the gods to visit mortals; and he was afraid to condemn Jesus, for fear of offending some of the supreme deities. Perhaps the question in the succeeding verse refers to this.
entries.f7b20e61c2e48e9b154e758d65852c99972bfb23: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen42995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42996" type="x-p"/> Whence art thou? - This certainly does not mean, From what country art thou? for Pilate knew this well enough; but it appears he made this inquiry to know who were the parents of Christ; what were his pretensions, and whether he really were a demigod, such as the heathens believed in. To this question we find our Lord gave no answer. He had already told him that his kingdom was not of this world; and that he came to erect a spiritual kingdom, not a temporal one: <reference osisRef="Joh.18.36">Joh 18:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.18.37">Joh 18:37</reference>. This answer he deemed sufficient; and he did not choose to satisfy a criminal curiosity, nor to enter then into any debate concerning the absurdity of the heathen worship.
