The local situation served also to prove the truth of his resurrection, and to throw no small light on the narrative which is contained in the following chapter.
CHAPTER 20.
John 20:1-9
1. Now, on;he first day of the week,
“Or le premier (des join’s) du Sabbath, ou, le premier jour de la semaine;” — “Now, the first (of the days) of the Sabbath, or, the first day of the week.”
Mary Magdelene goeth early to the sepulcher, while it was, yet dark, and seeth the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. 2. Then she runneth, and cometh to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and saith to them, They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulcher, and we know not where they have laid him. 3. Peter therefore went forth, and the other disciple, and came to the sepulcher. 4. And they both ran together, and the other disciple outran Peter, and came first to the sepulchre. 5. And, stooping down, he saw the linen clothes lying; yet he went not in. 6. Then Simon Peter came following him, and entered into the sepulcher, and saw the linen clothes lying; 7. And the napkin that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself. 8. Then the other disciple, who came first to the sepulcher, went in also, and he saw and believed. 9. For as yet they knew not the scripture, that tie must must rise from the dead.

entries.a059083b81f171c1c3f5d3d960aa780361cb8aa5:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="19" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XIX.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p>THen <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.29. Mark 15.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Pilate therefore took Jesus, and scourg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It was the custom of the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> when any one was to be Crucified, first to scourge him; but (as it appears) <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> ordered it, hoping, that tho he could not prevail by any other art with them, yet by this he might, and they might possibly be satisfied with this lighter punishment; for it appeareth by <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 4th and 12th. that <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> had a mind to release him, if he could have satisfied the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> tho he had not courage enough to oppose the stream, and to do what himself thought was just, in despight of their oppo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sition.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And the souldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put it on his head, and they put on him a purple robe <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The other Evangelists also mention a <ns0:hi>reed</ns0:hi> put into his right hand; the Crown, and the Purple <ns0:hi>Robe,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>Scepter,</ns0:hi> are all <ns0:hi>regal Ensigns,</ns0:hi> they give them to Christ in derision of his pretence to a Kingdom, and in the mean time themselves proclaim what he had said, That his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom was not of this World; for tho earthly Kings wear Crowns, yet they use to be of Gold, not of Thorns; and their Scepters use to be <ns0:hi>Gold,</ns0:hi> not Reeds.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And said, Hail, King of the Jews: and they smote him with their hands <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">when they said, <ns0:hi>Hail king of the Iews</ns0:hi>; but yet spake a great truth, (tho not in their sense) The other Evangelists speak of more indignities offered him. (See the notes on <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 15.19.)</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">They mockt him</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Pilate therefore went forth again, and saith unto them, Behold, I bring him forth to you, that ye may know that I find no fault in him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> appeareth convinced in his own conscience, that Christ had done nothing worthy either of death or bonds, and a great while resisted that strong temptation which he was under, to please the people, and to secure his own sta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, lest any complaint made to the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Emperor against him should have prejudiced him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> saith unto them, Behold the man <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He therefore, after Jesus had been scourged, and dres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed up in this mock-dress, brings him out again to the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple to move their pity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 When the chief priests therefore, and offi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cers saw him, they cried out, saying, Crucifie <ns0:hi>hmi,</ns0:hi> crucifie <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Our Lord findeth more compassion from <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> (tho an <ns0:hi>Heathen</ns0:hi>) than he found from those of his own Nation; yea, those that pretended highest to Religion amongst them<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> would have saved him, they cry out for his blood.</ns0:note>. Pilate saith unto them, Take ye <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and crucifie him: for I find no fault in him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> leaves another testimony behind him, that what he did at last overborn with a great Temptation, he did con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trary to the conviction of his own conscience, and as yet de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clineth the guilt of innocent blood.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 The Jews answered him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 24.16.</ns0:note>, We have a law <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Law they mean, is the Law for putting <ns0:hi>false Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets</ns0:hi> to death, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 18.20.</ns0:note>, and by our law he ought to die, because <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Chap. 5.18. and 10.33.</ns0:note> he made himself the Son of God <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>Son of God here,</ns0:hi> they mean the eternal Son of God, in all things equal with his Father; otherwise it was a term applicable to themselves, whom God calls his Son, his first-born, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> now for any in this sense to arrogate to himself this title, who indeed was not so, was Blasphemy, and that in the highest degree, and brought him under the notion of a <ns0:hi>false Prophet</ns0:hi> of the deepest dye: but this was injuriously applied to Christ, who thought it no robbery to be equal with the Father, and who was so declared by God himself at his <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Transfi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guration</ns0:hi>; and who had made his Divine Power appear by such works as no meer man ever did.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he was the more afraid <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It should seem, that the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> permitted Judgments to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> according to their own Laws, which the <ns0:hi>Roman Governor</ns0:hi> was to see executed; or else seeing the rabble in such an heat and disorder, he feared some breaking out.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And went again into the judgment hall, and saith unto Jesus, Whence art thou? But Jesus gave him no answer <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Our Lord, who knew the secrets of all mens hearts, very well knew, that tho <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> had for some time with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood his temptations, yet he would at last yeild; he also was ready to lay down his life, as he knew was determined for him; having therefore made a reasonable defence, he thinks fit to add no more of that nature.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not, that I have pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er to crucifie thee, and have power to release thee <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> seemeth something displeased, that Christ would be no more free; men in Worldly power, are too prone to forget from whom they derive it.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Our Lord checketh <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> modestly for boasting of his Authority as a Judge to absolve or condemn him; de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />claring, that all the power he had was derived from God, who in his eternal Counsels had determined this thing, which must therefore come to pass:</ns0:note>: therefore he that delivered me unto thee, hath the greater sin <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">But withal lets him know, that this neither excused him, nor muchless the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who were to execute the Divine purposes. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> was to look to Gods revealed Will, not his secret Counsels, of which he could have no knowledge; but he saith, they who had de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered him to him had the greater sin; he did act but as a Judge upon their accusations, they procured the false witness, they would not be satisfied without his blood, and they sinned against much more light.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He sought all fair and plausible means to release him, being convinced in his own conscience, that he was an in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nocent man:</ns0:note>: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Cesars friend <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">but the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> double their clamors, and (ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the usual acts of Sycophants) quit their charge as to Religion, tho that was the true and real cause of all their malice; and pursue onely the charge which was pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per for the Cognisance of the <ns0:hi>Roman Governor</ns0:hi> of Sed<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tion or Rebellion, and tacitly accuse <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> as a Traytor, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing false to his trust, if he should let our Saviour go; for no man could set up himself as a King, but he must proclaim himself a Traytor to the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Emperor.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 17.7.</ns0:note>: Who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever maketh himself a king, speaketh against Cesar.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:369" />13 ¶ When Pilate therefore heard that saying <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That saying, that if he let Jesus go, he was not <ns0:hi>Cesars</ns0:hi> friend. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> was a man that loved the honour that was from men, more than the honour and praise which is from God; and was more afraid of losing his place than his Soul, and could no longer resist the temptation he was under:</ns0:note>, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment-seat, in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">he brought forth Christ, and sate down in a place called the <ns0:hi>Pavement,</ns0:hi> because it was paved with stone, but in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> (mixed with the <ns0:hi>Syriack) Gabbatha,</ns0:hi> that is, an <ns0:hi>High place</ns0:hi>; for it was their manner to have their <ns0:hi>Iudg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment-seats</ns0:hi> higher than other parts of the room where they were.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And it was the preparation of the passover <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The preparation to any feast, signifies the day before it, because on that day they prepared whatsoever accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the Law was necessary for the Solemnization. Some much doubt, whither in this place the <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> signifies strictly the <ns0:hi>Paschal Supper,</ns0:hi> which it could not do, if the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> strictly this year kept to the Law; for the fourteenth day of the month <ns0:hi>Nisan</ns0:hi> at evening, was the time when most certainly Christ kept it, who ate it the night before. It is therefore more probably thought, that by the <ns0:hi>Passover</ns0:hi> here, is meant their great Festival, which was upon the fifteenth day. (See the notes on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 18.28.)</ns0:note>, and about the sixth hour <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> tells us it was about the sixth hour; that is, in the latter part of the interval, between nine a clock in the morning, and twelve at noon: for the division of the day according to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> was in four parts; the first was from the rising of the Sun, till our nine in the morning, and was called the third hour; the other was from the third hour to the sixt, that is twelve a clock at noon; the third division was from their sixt hour to the ninth, that is, three a clock with us in the afternoon; the fourth division was from the ninth hour to Sunset, that is with us six a clock in the evening, when the Sun is in the Equinox. Now, not onely the time when any of these hours came, was called either the third or sixt hour; but the space of three hours alotted to each division, was so called when the next division began; so the time of our Saviours Crucifixion is recorded by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> to be the third hour: that is, the whole space from nine a clock to twelve, was not quite gone, tho it was near at an end. And by the Evangelist, here 'tis said, that it was a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout the sixt hour, that is near our twelve a clock. And thus the different relations are clearly recorded.</ns0:note>: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your king <ns0:hi>y.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But they cried out, Away with <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> away with <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> crucifie him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucifie your king<ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The more <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> sought to quiet them, the more they rage, contrary to all dictates of reason; when God hath determined a thing, all things shall concur to bring it about. <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> mocks them when he saith, shall I Crucifie your King?</ns0:note>? The chief priests answered <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 49.10</ns0:note>, We have no king but Cesar <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Yet so fierce was their malice against Christ, that to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel the Governor to condemn him, tho there were not a people under Heaven, more zealous for their liberties, nor more impatient of a forreign yoke; they cry out, <ns0:hi>We have no king but Cesar</ns0:hi>: That is, the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Emperor who had Conquered them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.26. Mark 15.15. Luke 23.24.</ns0:note> Then <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This must be at or about twelve of the clock, for that must be signified by the sixth hour, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14.</ns0:note> delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus and led him away <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demned him, and delivered him to the executioner, who (as the manner is in such cases) led him away.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And he bearing his cross went forth into a place, called <ns0:hi>the place</ns0:hi> of a scull, which is called in the Hebrew, Golgotha <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.31, 32, 33. Where, what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever needs expounding on this Verse, may be found, and this Text is reconciled to that; which telleth us, that one <ns0:hi>Simon,</ns0:hi> a man of <ns0:hi>Cyrene,</ns0:hi> bare his Cross. Their places of Execution (as usually with us) were without their Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Where they crucified him, and two others with him, on either side one, and Jesus in the midst.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 38.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 15.26. Luke 23.38.</ns0:note> Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ESUS OF NA<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth</ns0:hi> 27.38.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 This tit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>e then read many of the Jews: for the place where Jesus was crucified was nigh to the city <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As all their places of Execution were within two fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longs, or thereabouts:</ns0:note>: and it was written in Hebrew, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Greek, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Latin <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">it was wrote in all three Langua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges, that not the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> onely, but all such strangers as were come up to the Feast, might understand it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Then said the chief priests of the Jews to Pilate, write not, The king of the Jews; but that he said, I am king of the Jews <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> thought it would be a disgrace to them, that Christ should be reported abroad as their King<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> therefore they desire an alteration of the writing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Pilate answered, What I have written, I have written <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">But <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> refuseth to gratifie them, and lets them know he would not be directed by them what to write, nor alter any thing of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 23.34.</ns0:note> Then the souldiers, when they had cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every souldier a part and also <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> coat: now the coat was without seam <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> wroug<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t.</ns0:note>, woven from the top throughout <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Both <ns0:hi>Matthew Chap.</ns0:hi> 27.35. aand <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 15.24. men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion this parting of Christs garments amongst them, which must be understood of his inward garments; which some tell us might easily be done, because their garments were made up of four parts, but his outward garment which is called his coat, was all of a piece.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rent it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be: that the scripture might be fu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>filled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the souldiers did <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This made them chuse rather to cast lots for that, than to divide it, as they had done his inward garments. But there was something more in it than the Souldiers knew; Christ hereby proved a true <ns0:hi>Antitype</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> who said of himself figuratively, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22.18. <ns0:hi>They part my garments amongst them, and cast lots upon my vesture</ns0:hi>; by which he meant no more, than that his enemies loaded them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves with his spoils: those words which figuratively were true of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> proved literally true as to Christ. Thus vile and wicked men are fulfilling the Scriptures, when they lit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle think of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 ¶ <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.55. Mark 15.40. Luke 23.49.</ns0:note> Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother, and his mothers sister, Mary <ns0:hi>the wife</ns0:hi> of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Cleopa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Cleophas and Mary Magdalen <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">These words [<ns0:hi>the wife</ns0:hi>] are not in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> but supplied by our Translators; which leaves it doubtful, whi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther that <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>the wife,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Mother,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Daugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of Cleophas.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap, 13.23. and 21.24.</ns0:note> disciple standing by, whom he loved <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">We <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> often heard that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was the beloved Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and u<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ally expressed under the Notion of him whom Jesus loved<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note>, he saith unto his mother, VVoman, behold thy son <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Our Lord commendeth his Mother to the care of <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> whom he had ordered to take care of her, as if he had been her own Son<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> this letteth us know, that <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> was at <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>his time dead, otherwise, it is not probable, that Christ would have committed his Mother to any other Guardian.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother. And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own <ns0:hi>home</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He also reciprocally commendeth his Mother to <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> to be cared for as his own Mother. From that time <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> went home, and lived with <ns0:hi>Iohn.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 ¶ After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished that the scripture might be fulfilled <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 69.21.</ns0:note>, saith, I thirst.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Now there was set a vessel full of vineger: And they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.48.</ns0:note> filled a spunge with vineger, and put it upon hyssope, and put it to his mouth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> said, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 69.21. to signifie his enemies mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiplying afflictions upon him, <ns0:hi>They gave me also gall for my meat, and in my thirst they gave me vineger to drink</ns0:hi>; which he spake metaphorically; part of these words were without a figure literally fulfilled in Christ, who was the Son of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>; for he crying out upon the Cross that he thirsted, there being no other liquor at hand, or this being set on purpose for this end, they dip a spunge in it, and give it to him to drink; whither to stupifie his senses, or to prolong his life in those torments, or barely to quench his thirst, is hard to determine. It is probable, that it was such a kind of refreshment as they allowed to ordinary malefactors in his circumstances, the particulars of which usage we are not able to determine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:369" />30 When Jesus therefore had received the vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neger, he said <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17.4.</ns0:note>, It is finished <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">When Christ had tasted the vineger, he said, <ns0:hi>It is fini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shed.</ns0:hi> That is, I have now done and suffered all things which lay upon me in this life to do and suffer.</ns0:note>: And he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Having said this, he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.</ns0:hi> They are terms expressive of death; and our Saviours free surren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der of his Soul unto his Father.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 The Jews therefore because it was the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paration <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It was the <ns0:hi>Preparation,</ns0:hi> not to the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> (for that was celebrated the night before) but to the weekly Sab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bath; and they judged according to the Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 21.23. <ns0:hi>that the land would be defiled,</ns0:hi> if the persons executed were not buried that day; but their bodies should remain on the tree all night, especially on the Sabbath which began imme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diately after Sun-set.</ns0:note>, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath-day <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And this Sabbath was a more than ordinary Sabbath, for it was not onely the weekly Sabbath, but also their second day of unleavened bread; which, and the last day, were both very solemn days as may be seen, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 23.</ns0:note> (for that sabbath-day was an high day <ns0:hi>u</ns0:hi>) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> they might be taken away <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">This makes them come and beseech <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> that the bodies might be taken down, and in order to it, <ns0:hi>that their legs might be broken,</ns0:hi> lest any life remaining in them, they should revive and escape.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 Then came the souldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">They brake the two other malefactors legs, but not Christs, because they found him dead. Is is very possible in a natural course, that of three men dying in the same manner, one may die sooner then another; but it is but rationally presumed, that the cause of our Saviours quicker death, was not the failure of his spirits sooner, but his own voluntary surrender of his Soul.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 But one of the souldiers with a spear pierced his side <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">But one of the Souldiers to make sure of him, pierced his side, out of which it is said, that there presently came forth blood, and water: That there should come out blood is no wonder, nor yet that there should come forth water. Blood being congealed, it is ordinary to see water on the top of the Vessel where it is. And besides, Anatomists tells us, that in the hollow part of the breast, there are watery, as well as bloody humours in the membrane that incom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passeth the heart, which being pierced, and the water let out, the living creature dyeth necessarily. But yet in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard of the next words, <ns0:hi>He that saw it bare record, and he knoweth that he saith true,</ns0:hi> &c. most Divines think, that there was some mystery in this <ns0:hi>water</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>blood,</ns0:hi> which came out of Christs side pierced. Some would have the two <ns0:hi>Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />craments of the Gospel,</ns0:hi> signified by this <ns0:hi>water</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>blood.</ns0:hi> Christ 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.6. is said to have <ns0:hi>came by water and blood</ns0:hi>; That is, say Interpreters, be brought in a true <ns0:hi>expiation of sins</ns0:hi> by his blood, and the <ns0:hi>laver of Regeneration,</ns0:hi> washing the Soul from its filthiness: And thus he proved the true <ns0:hi>Antitype,</ns0:hi> answering the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Types in <ns0:hi>Sacrifices, and di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers washings.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and forthwith came there out, blood and water.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And he that saw it, bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Nor was this a fable, for <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saw it, and bare record, and knew it to be true, and published it, that men might believe that he was he, in whom all the legal Types and Fi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gures had their complement.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 For these things were done, that the scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture might be fulfilled <ns0:note place="margin">Psal. 34.20.</ns0:note>, A bone of him shall not be broken <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Nor was there any thing of this, but in fulfilling of the Scripture; for it was Gods Law about the Passover, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12.46. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 9.12. concerning the <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb,</ns0:hi> (which was a Type of Christ, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.29. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.7.) <ns0:hi>that a bone of it should not be broken.</ns0:hi> So as by this breaking no bone of Christs body, they might have understood, that he was figured out by the <ns0:hi>Paschal Lamb.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">So also by seeing Christs <ns0:hi>side pierced,</ns0:hi> (a thing not very usual) they might have understood, that he was the person mentioned, <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 12.10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 ¶ And after this Joseph of Aramithea (be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap 9 22. and 12.42.</ns0:note> fear of the Jews) besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave: He came therefore and took the body of Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sus.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.57, 58, 59.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And there came also Nicodemus which at the first came to Jesus by night <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The History of <ns0:hi>Nicodemus</ns0:hi> coming by night to our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour, and of their discourse together, we had <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 3.9, 10. We again heard of him standing up for <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>San<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hedrim, Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.50. We read no more of him till now, where he shews his love to his dead body;</ns0:note> and brought a mixture of myrrhe and aloes, about an hundred pound <ns0:hi>weight</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">bringing an hundred pound weight of <ns0:hi>Myrrhe</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Alo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s,</ns0:hi> which were both of them druggs used in embalming dead bodies, as also in perfuming other things, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linnen clothes, with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That is, persons of fashion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 Now in the place where he was crucified, there was a garden <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">their burial places; which usually were <ns0:hi>Vaults,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Caves</ns0:hi> within the Earth.</ns0:note>; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">their burial places; which usually were <ns0:hi>Vaults,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Caves</ns0:hi> within the Earth.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">As all their gardens were out of the City, as also</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 There laid they Jesus therefore, because of the Jews preparation-<ns0:hi>day,</ns0:hi> for the sepulchre was nigh at hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">There they immediately buried Christ, because the time, strictly called the <ns0:hi>Preparation</ns0:hi> (for the whole day was so called) was nigh at hand. See a fuller account of the History of our Saviours Passion, Death and Burial, in the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. where what is said by all the Evangelists, is compared together, and made one compleat History.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
            </ns0:div>
